title: If we really went to the moon in 1969, why haven't we been back since 1972? Think about it.
content:
Ok so let me get this straight. In 1969 we had computers weaker than a Tamagotchi, suits held together with basically duct tape, and rockets designed by a literal former Nazi scientist (look up Operation Paperclip, it's real) — and we NAILED IT on the first try. Six successful landings. Zero problems. Then in 1972 we just... stopped. And in the 50+ years since, with technology that is literally millions of times more powerful, we just... can't go back?

NASA themselves admitted they "destroyed the technology" and "it would be painful to build it back." Their words not mine. You don't "destroy" technology that works. You iterate on it. Unless it never existed in the first place.

Let's talk about the Van Allen radiation belts. These are bands of intense radiation surrounding Earth that should have absolutely fried the astronauts. NASA's official explanation is basically "they went through it really fast." Oh ok cool, I'll just drive through a wall really fast next time.

And the footage. Oh man, the footage. The flag "waving" in a vacuum. The multiple light sources when the sun should be the only one. The identical backgrounds in photos that were supposedly taken miles apart. The fact that the original high-quality tapes were "accidentally erased" in the 1980s. Who accidentally erases the most important footage in human history?

Stanley Kubrick released 2001: A Space Odyssey in 1968 — one year before the "landing." The man literally invented front-projection technology for that film. And then NASA just happened to pull off the real thing 12 months later looking suspiciously similar? The Shining is Kubrick's confession. Room 237. The Apollo 11 sweater on Danny. Do your own research.

I'm not saying space isn't real. I'm saying we didn't go to the moon in 1969. And the fact that they won't go back tells you everything you need to know.

title: We are 18 months from AGI and nobody is acting like it. Why?
content:
I have been reading every major paper that's come out in the last 6 months. I'm talking the o3 benchmarks, the Gemini 2.5 architecture leaks, the stuff DeepMind quietly dropped on arxiv at 2am on a Friday. These systems are scoring 90th percentile on the BAR exam, writing publishable code, and PLANNING MULTI-STEP TASKS WITH TOOL USE. That's not autocomplete. That's not a stochastic parrot. That is general reasoning.

And yet I go to work on Monday and my manager is asking me to fill out a Jira ticket for a CSS fix. I talk to my friends and they're worried about mortgage rates. My dad asked me if ChatGPT can help him write a birthday card.

WE ARE STARING DOWN THE BARREL OF THE MOST TRANSFORMATIVE EVENT IN HUMAN HISTORY AND PEOPLE ARE STILL ARGUING ABOUT WHETHER AI CAN "REALLY" THINK.

Let me put it this way: 3 years ago these models couldn't reliably count the letters in a word. Now they're solving novel PhD-level mathematics problems and discovering protein structures. The trajectory is not ambiguous. The slope of that curve does not lead to "slightly better chatbot." It leads to something that makes every knowledge worker on earth redundant within a decade.

But sure. Let's keep posting memes about AI art having too many fingers.

I feel like I'm taking crazy pills. I genuinely do not understand why people aren't in the streets over this. Not protesting — just ACKNOWLEDGING that the world is about to fundamentally change. Are we all just too tired? Is it a coping mechanism? Did we collectively decide that if we don't look at the freight train it won't hit us?

Someone please tell me I'm wrong because I would love to be wrong right now.

title: Google just mass-fired 12,000 people and then posted a job listing for a 'Chief Happiness Officer.' I am not making this up.
content:
I genuinely thought this was satire when someone on my team Slacked it to me. Google lays off 12,000 people — via EMAIL, mind you, not even a call — and then the SAME WEEK posts a role for a Chief Happiness Officer with a compensation band of $350-450K. The job description literally includes 'fostering a culture of psychological safety and belonging.' BELONGING. For the people who still have badge access, I guess.

But here's the part that actually broke me. They removed the free kombucha from the microkitchens on the same day they announced the layoffs. The kombucha. That's like burning down your house and also canceling the newspaper subscription. It's not even a cost-saving measure at that point, it's performance art.

Meanwhile Sundar's total comp last year was $226 MILLION. You know what $226 million buys? Roughly 2,260 engineers at $100K each. But no, we needed that money for... checks notes... a CEO who sends emails titled 'A difficult decision' while sitting on a yacht that has a smaller yacht inside it.

My favorite part is the Googlers who are STILL defending this. 'Oh but the severance package is generous.' Brother, they gave people 16 weeks and then blacklisted their badge before they could even grab their desk plant. Karen from People Ops sent a follow-up email about returning your Chromebook with a smiley face emoji. A SMILEY FACE.

The tech industry isn't a meritocracy. It's a cargo cult where we worship ping pong tables and pretend stock refreshers are a personality trait. The Chief Happiness Officer position is still open btw. I'm sure they'll find someone great right after they finish escorting the last batch of laid-off employees past the nap pods.

title: MIT did a study "debunking" tin foil hats and it was FUNDED BY THE GOVERNMENT. Do I need to draw you a picture?
content:
Every time someone brings up tin foil hats, some redditor links the MIT study from 2005 like it's the final word on the matter. "AcTuAlLy TiN fOiL hAtS aMpLiFy SiGnAlS." Yeah. That's exactly what they'd want you to think.

Let's think about this for two seconds. Who funds MIT? Federal grants. Who distributes federal grants? The government. So the government funded a study at one of their top research universities that concluded the ONE low-cost method of blocking electromagnetic signals actually makes things worse. How convenient.

And notice what they did — they didn't say "foil hats do nothing." They said foil hats AMPLIFY certain government frequencies. Translation: "Please stop wearing them, they're making our signals stronger, we definitely aren't worried about you blocking anything." That's not debunking. That's reverse psychology. That's a psy-op.

Why does every movie, every TV show, every piece of media portray tin foil hat wearers as crazy? Because it's the most effective form of discrediting in human history. You don't have to disprove the method — you just have to make anyone who uses it look insane. It costs them nothing and it works on 99% of people.

Here are things we KNOW are real: the government has technology that can beam sounds directly into your skull (look up the microwave auditory effect — it's declassified). Cell towers broadcast in the exact frequency ranges that aluminum attenuates. And the first person to write about foil hats — Julian Huxley — was the brother of Aldous Huxley, who wrote BRAVE NEW WORLD, a book about a government that controls its population's thoughts. Coincidence? COINCIDENCE?

I'm not telling you to wear a tin foil hat. I'm telling you to ask yourself why they spent so much money and cultural capital convincing you not to. That's all. Think about it.

title: I work at a Fortune 500 and our entire legal team just got replaced by an AI pipeline. This is happening NOW.
content:
Throwaway for obvious reasons. I'm a mid-level PM at a company you've definitely heard of. Fortune 200 actually. I won't say which one but we're in financial services.

Last quarter the C-suite approved a pilot to use an AI pipeline for contract review. Standard stuff right? NDA review, redlining, compliance checks against our internal policies. The pilot was supposed to take 6 months. It took 3 weeks. Not 3 weeks to build — 3 weeks to OUTPERFORM the existing team on every metric. Speed, accuracy, consistency. It caught a liability clause in a vendor agreement that our senior counsel had missed for two consecutive renewal cycles.

So what happened next? They expanded it. Discovery, regulatory filings, internal compliance audits. They built an orchestration layer where one model reads the documents, another checks against case law, and a third generates the actual legal briefs. A human "reviews" at the end but I've watched the review meetings. The partner glances at it for 45 seconds and signs off.

We had 340 people in legal. We now have 97. And I'm hearing the next round is coming in Q2.

The part that broke my brain? My buddy Marcus — 8 years at the company, Georgetown Law, genuinely brilliant guy — got his severance package generated by the same AI system that replaced him. He told me over beers. He wasn't even mad anymore. Just this thousand-yard stare. "It wrote a better severance letter than I would have," he said.

I keep seeing people online saying AI is overhyped, it can't do REAL work, it hallucinates too much. Brother I am WATCHING it do real work. The hallucination rate on our pipeline is 0.3% after fine-tuning on our internal docs. Our human error rate was 4.2%. Those numbers ended careers.

This is not coming. It is HERE. It happened at my company and it is happening at every major firm I talk to at conferences. The only people who don't know are the ones about to find out the hard way.

I am not okay.

title: I've been a software engineer for 20 years. The mass layoffs aren't about the economy. They're about shareholders finally realizing engineers aren't magic.
content:
I started coding professionally in 2006. I've survived three recessions, two dot-com aftershocks, and the mass delusion that was the blockchain hiring spree of 2017. What's happening now isn't a downturn. It's a CORRECTION, and frankly it's been coming for a while.

Here's what actually happened. From 2020 to 2022, interest rates were basically zero. Money was free. VCs were throwing cash at anything with a landing page and a Notion doc. And Big Tech? They went on the most absurd hiring binge in the history of capitalism. Google hired 60,000 people in two years. META hired so many people that new engineers would show up on their first day and literally have no team to join. They called it 'resting and vesting.' That was an ACTUAL TERM people used WITH A STRAIGHT FACE.

We hired 400 people to build a feature that 3 people could have shipped. The 3 people who could have shipped it spent 18 months in alignment meetings with the other 397. I personally attended a meeting about scheduling a meeting to discuss the roadmap for a planning meeting. That is not a joke. I have the calendar invite.

The dirty secret is that most of those hires weren't about building things. They were about DENYING TALENT TO COMPETITORS. It was a Cold War strategy applied to software engineers. 'If we hire all the good React developers, our competitors can't.' Except they hired a LOT of not-good React developers too and nobody noticed because everyone was too busy writing their 'impact statements' for perf review.

Now rates are up, growth is slowing, and some finance person at every major tech company finally opened a spreadsheet and said 'wait, we have 14 people on the Developer Experience for Internal Tools Platform Infrastructure team and none of them can explain what they do?' SHOCKED PIKACHU FACE.

I feel for everyone who got laid off. I really do. But I also watched a 24-year-old with 8 months of experience turn down a $400K offer because it didn't include enough equity refreshers. The market was broken. This is it unbreaking. It just sucks that the people paying the price aren't the executives who created the problem in the first place.

title: I tried to drive to Bielefeld, Germany last summer. What happened next changed everything I thought I knew.
content:
So last July I was doing a road trip through Germany. Munich, Hamburg, Berlin, the usual. My buddy dared me to stop in Bielefeld because of the whole conspiracy thing. I thought it would be funny. Put it in Google Maps, got directions, started driving.

Here's where it gets weird. I was driving on the A2 autobahn, which supposedly goes right through Bielefeld. I set the GPS for the city center. About 30 km out, my GPS 'recalculated' and routed me around the city. I manually set it again. Recalculated AGAIN. I said screw it and just followed highway signs.

I saw a sign that said 'Bielefeld 15 km.' Then nothing. The next sign was for Herford. Bielefeld just... wasn't there anymore. I pulled over at a gas station and asked the attendant how to get to Bielefeld. He looked at me like I asked him where Narnia was and said 'just keep driving, you'll find it.' Helpful.

Now before you say 'you just missed the exit' -- I drove that stretch THREE TIMES. I have a master's degree. I can read highway signs. Something is not right.

And don't even get me started on the fact that the German government has NEVER officially denied the conspiracy. They joke about it. They laugh. You know what people do when they're hiding something? They make the truth sound like a joke so nobody takes it seriously.

330,000 people supposedly live there but have you EVER met someone from Bielefeld? Have you? Because I haven't. And I've been to Germany four times.

THEY don't want you asking questions. But I'm asking them anyway.

title: The scaling laws haven't broken. They just went quiet. Here's what that means.
content:
I've been in ML for about 8 years now. Did my PhD on optimization, spent time at one of the big labs (not saying which), now I'm at a startup. I follow the papers religiously. And there's something that's been bugging me for the last year that I think most people outside the field haven't noticed.

The scaling papers stopped.

Think about this. From 2020-2023 we got a flood of landmark work on scaling laws. Kaplan et al. showed that performance scales predictably with compute, data, and parameters. Chinchilla refined the optimal ratios. Every few months someone would drop a paper showing the curves keep going up. It was the most important empirical finding in modern ML: intelligence is a function of scale, and the function is remarkably smooth and predictable.

Then around mid-2024 it just... went quiet. OpenAI stopped publishing. Google got vague. Anthropic released Constitutional AI stuff but nothing about where their curves were going. Meta put out Llama but conspicuously left out the scaling analysis.

The popular narrative became "scaling laws are hitting a wall" and "we need new paradigms." Tech Twitter ran with it. VCs repeated it. Journalists wrote the obituary for scaling.

But here's the thing: NOBODY PUBLISHED EVIDENCE THAT SCALING BROKE. The wall narrative came from vibes, not data. What actually happened is the labs stopped sharing their scaling data right around the point where the curves would have shown capabilities that are... let's say commercially and strategically sensitive.

I still talk to people at these labs. Not about anything proprietary — I'm not trying to get anyone fired. But the general sentiment I get is not "scaling hit a wall." It's more like nervous laughter and subject changes. One friend told me "the curves are fine" and then immediately said he shouldn't have said that.

Now think about what's happened since: o3 solving novel math competition problems. Models that can genuinely write and debug complex software. Systems that do multi-hour research tasks autonomously. Where do you think those capabilities came from? A breakthrough in architecture? No. They came from where the scaling curves said they would be.

They didn't stop publishing because the results were disappointing. They stopped publishing because the results were too good. You don't go quiet when your most important research direction fails. You go quiet when it succeeds and you realize what that means.

I don't think this is a conspiracy exactly. It's rational self-interest. If you're sitting on data showing that 10x more compute gives you something that can do most white-collar jobs, you don't publish that in a nice arxiv paper with reproducible methodology. You keep it internal and figure out how to monetize it before anyone else catches up.

The scaling laws didn't break. We just stopped being allowed to see them. And that should scare you more than if they had broken.

title: Apple just announced a product that already exists, called it revolutionary, and the stock went up 4%. I love this timeline.
content:
I just sat through the entire WWDC keynote and I need someone to explain to me how a room full of adults gasped — AUDIBLY GASPED — when Apple announced split-screen multitasking on iPad. Samsung has had this since 2013. That's not a typo. Two thousand and thirteen. The feature is old enough to be in middle school.

But here's the Apple magic. They didn't call it split-screen. They called it 'Fluid Spatial Multitasking' and showed a 4-minute animation of windows gracefully gliding across the screen while a woman in a tastefully lit loft apartment pretended to be productive. And you know what? The stock went up 4%. Four percent. That's roughly $100 billion in market cap because they discovered what Android did during the Obama administration.

The real MVP of every Apple keynote is Craig Federighi. This man's hair deserves its own segment. It deserves its own KEYNOTE. He walks out there with that silver mane flowing like he just stepped off a shampoo commercial and the crowd goes nuts. He could announce that iOS is removing the phone app and people would clap. 'We think you're going to love it.'

My personal favorite moment was when they announced RCS support and framed it as Apple being generous and caring about interoperability. Brother, the EU literally FORCED you to do this. That's like a bank robber returning the money and calling himself a philanthropist. Tim Cook stood there with his hands clasped like a benevolent monk and said 'we believe in connecting everyone' as if they hadn't spent a decade deliberately making green bubble texts look like garbage to shame Android users into switching.

Also they showed a demo of an AI feature that hallucinated wrong information DURING THE KEYNOTE and nobody on stage acknowledged it. The presenter just smiled and moved on. Confidence level: sociopathic. I respect it.

I'm still going to buy everything they announced. I'm part of the problem. We all are. See you at the Apple Store on launch day, you beautiful sheep.

title: The government has changed the Roswell story FOUR TIMES since 1947. Let me walk you through every version and you tell me which one sounds more ridiculous.
content:
Let's play a game. I'll list every official explanation the U.S. government has given for what crashed at Roswell, and you tell me if this sounds like an organization that's telling the truth.

Version 1 (July 8, 1947): The Army issues a press release saying they recovered a 'flying disc.' Their words. Not mine. Not some conspiracy website. The ACTUAL UNITED STATES MILITARY said they found a flying disc.

Version 2 (July 9, 1947): ONE DAY LATER, they change the story. Now it's a weather balloon. They hold a press conference with balloon debris that looks nothing like what the witnesses described. General Ramey literally posed for photos with substitute materials.

Version 3 (1994): After 47 years of 'weather balloon,' the Air Force suddenly says actually it was a Project Mogul balloon. A classified nuclear detection balloon. Oh so it WASN'T a weather balloon? So you lied for 47 years? Cool cool cool.

Version 4 (1997): The Air Force publishes ANOTHER report to explain the 'alien bodies' witnesses reported. Their explanation? Crash test dummies dropped from high altitude in the 1950s. Except the Roswell crash was in 1947. The dummy drops started in 1953. SIX YEARS LATER. The Air Force's official explanation is that witnesses confused events from different DECADES. That's their story.

Now let's look at what the witnesses actually said. Jesse Marcel, the intelligence officer who first examined the debris, went to his grave saying it was not from any balloon. Multiple witnesses described metallic material that couldn't be bent, cut, or burned. Brazel's son said the debris had properties unlike anything he'd ever seen.

Four stories in 50 years. Each one contradicting the last. And somehow I'M the crazy one for asking questions. They don't want you thinking about this. They want you to accept Version 4 and move on. But if they've lied three times already, why would the fourth time be the truth?

Connect the dots. Or don't. They're counting on you not to.

title: OpenAI employees keep quitting and nobody is asking the right questions about what they saw
content:
Let me just lay out a timeline and you can tell me if this seems normal.

2023: Jan Leike and the entire superalignment team leave OpenAI. Leike posts a thread saying safety has been "taking a backseat" and he's lost confidence the company will handle it responsibly. Ilya Sutskever — co-founder, chief scientist, the guy who arguably understood the models better than anyone alive — quietly departs after the board drama.

2024: Multiple safety-focused researchers leave. Some go to Anthropic, some go to smaller labs, some leave AI entirely. Daniel Kokotajlo gives up his equity — we're talking potentially millions of dollars — rather than sign a non-disparagement agreement. Think about what it takes to walk away from that kind of money just to preserve your right to speak freely.

Early 2025: More departures. The pattern continues. People who were deeply embedded in the most advanced AI research on the planet, who saw what the next generation of models could do before anyone else, are choosing to LEAVE.

Now the standard explanation is "tech turnover" and "disagreements about commercialization." And sure, some of it probably is that. People leave companies all the time.

But let me ask you something: when the lead safety researcher at a nuclear plant quits and says the plant isn't taking safety seriously enough, do we just say "oh well, turnover happens"? When multiple senior engineers leave Boeing and talk about quality concerns, is that just normal churn?

The equity clawback stuff is what gets me. OpenAI had provisions where departing employees could lose their vested equity if they didn't sign incredibly restrictive NDAs. They walked that back after public pressure but the fact that it existed tells you something. What are you trying to keep people from saying? If everything is fine and the technology is just a better chatbot, why do you need legal mechanisms to silence departing researchers?

I keep hearing people say "if it were really dangerous someone would blow the whistle." Brother, people ARE blowing the whistle. They're just doing it in the weird constrained way that people blow whistles when they're bound by NDAs and non-disparagement agreements. They leave. They give up money. They post cryptic threads. They join competitors focused on safety. They testify before Congress in careful measured language.

When the people building the thing start running, maybe we should ask why. When they sacrifice millions of dollars for the right to speak freely and then STILL choose their words extremely carefully, maybe the answer to "what did they see" is worse than we think.

I'm not saying AGI is here. I'm not saying the models are sentient or whatever. I'm saying that the people with the most information are acting like something significant is happening and the rest of us are pattern-matching their behavior to normal tech drama because the alternative is too uncomfortable.

Stop asking if AGI is coming. Start asking why the people who would know first are acting the way they're acting.

title: My startup raised $50M at a $500M valuation. We have 6 customers and one of them is my mom. AMA.
content:
Before you ask: yes, my mom pays full price. She's actually our highest-engagement user. She logs in every day and leaves comments like 'great job sweetie!' on the dashboard. Our investor deck lists her as a 'power user in the 55+ demographic.'

Here's how we did it. Step one: put 'AI-powered' on every single slide. Our pitch deck says AI-powered 14 times. Our AI is an if-else statement and a call to the OpenAI API with temperature set to 0.7. One of our 'proprietary models' is literally a regex. The VCs LOVED it. One partner at Andreessen told me our 'AI moat' was the strongest he'd seen all quarter. Our moat is an API key.

Step two: metrics gymnastics. We don't say 'users,' we say 'activated accounts.' We don't say 'revenue,' we say 'ARR trajectory based on contracted intent.' One of our 6 customers signed a letter of intent that is, legally speaking, worth nothing. We count it as $2M in pipeline. Our CFO — who is also me — calls this 'forward-looking accounting.' My actual accountant calls it 'concerning.'

Step three: buzzword bingo. Our product is a 'vertically-integrated, AI-native, API-first platform enabling enterprise-grade workflow orchestration for cross-functional stakeholder alignment.' It's a to-do list app. It has checkboxes. The checkboxes are nice though, they have a satisfying little animation when you click them. That animation cost $4M in engineering time.

The fundraise itself was a fever dream. We did a roadshow where I pitched 47 VCs in two weeks. I wore the same Patagonia vest to every meeting because someone told me it 'signals operator energy.' Three firms got into a bidding war over our round. None of them asked to see the product. NOT ONE. One partner told me, 'We invest in founders, not products.' Sir, the founder is a 32-year-old whose last startup was a Slack bot that nobody used.

We're using the $50M to hire 80 engineers, open an office in San Francisco that we'll use three days a week, and build an AI feature that does what our product already does but 'with intelligence.' Our burn rate is $1.2M per month. At this rate, we have roughly 41 months of runway, which I'm told is 'efficient' because at least we're not spending $3M a month like the OTHER to-do list startup that raised $120M.

Anyway, we're hiring. DM me if you want equity in a company that will either be worth $2 billion or absolutely nothing. There is no in-between.

title: I don't care about politics left or right but can someone explain why they needed THREE YEARS to produce a birth certificate? Something doesn't sit right.
content:
Look I need to preface this by saying I'm not political. I don't care about Democrat vs Republican. This isn't about that. This is about asking a simple question and watching the most powerful government on earth take THREE YEARS to answer it.

2008: People ask to see the birth certificate. Simple request. Every president could do this in about five minutes. Instead we get a 'Certificate of Live Birth' which is NOT the same thing as a birth certificate. It's a short-form digital printout. Any Hawaiian could get one. It proves nothing about WHERE you were born.

2009: Still no long-form certificate. 2010: Still nothing. Media calls anyone who asks a 'conspiracy theorist.' Classic. Shut down the question instead of answering it.

April 2011: FINALLY releases the long-form birth certificate. Three years later. And it just happens to be right before the 2012 campaign season. Convenient timing.

Now here's what nobody talks about. His grandmother — his OWN grandmother in Kenya — said in a recorded interview that she was present at his birth IN KENYA. The media immediately 'debunked' this by saying it was a translation error. She spoke in Swahili and supposedly meant something different. Right. A grandmother says she saw her grandson born and we're blaming Google Translate.

And the newspaper announcements from 1961? Anyone can submit a birth announcement. His grandparents lived in Hawaii. They could have called it in from anywhere. That's not proof, that's a phone call.

I'm not saying anything definitive. I'm just saying when someone takes three years to show you an ID, maybe it's because they were working on it. Do your own research. Look at the documents yourself. Don't let the media tell you what to think.

And before you call me a conspiracy theorist — I literally just asked a question.

title: If you're not terrified by recursive self-improvement you haven't thought about it hard enough
content:
I had a conversation with Claude last week that broke something in my brain and I haven't been able to put it back together. We weren't even talking about anything profound — I was asking it to help me optimize a function in my codebase. And it did. It made the code better. Measurably, objectively better than what I wrote.

Then I had this thought: what if it could do that to itself?

Not to its own source code necessarily. But to the PROCESS. To the training pipeline, the architecture, the reward functions, the data curation. What if you pointed a sufficiently capable AI at the problem of "make AI more capable" and it succeeded?

Let me walk you through why this keeps me up at night.

Step 1: You have an AI that's roughly human-level at AI research. Not better than the best researchers — just average. Just competent.

Step 2: That AI suggests improvements to training. Some work, some don't. The ones that work make the next version slightly smarter.

Step 3: The slightly smarter version is now better at suggesting improvements. So the NEXT round of improvements is larger.

Step 4: Repeat.

Do you see the problem? Each cycle the thing doing the improving gets better at improving. The gap between iterations doesn't stay constant — it GROWS. It's compound interest but for intelligence.

Imagine you taught a dog to selectively breed smarter dogs. You'd get slightly smarter dogs over many generations. Slow, manageable, fine. Now imagine the dogs figure out how to do the breeding program themselves. And each generation of smarter dogs runs a better breeding program. And they reproduce every 2 hours instead of every 2 years. How many cycles before you have something you can't control? How many cycles before the dogs are smarter than you?

Now replace "dogs" with a system that runs on servers and can copy itself and operates at the speed of electricity instead of biology.

"But there will be diminishing returns!" Maybe. Probably, even. But diminishing returns on an exponential curve can still be incomprehensibly fast in absolute terms. Even if each improvement is half as large as the last one, the sum still diverges if the cycles are fast enough.

"But we'll just turn it off!" Will we? Will we turn off the thing that's making companies billions of dollars? Will we turn off the thing that just cured a disease? Will every country on earth agree to turn it off simultaneously, including the ones using it for military advantage? Has humanity ever successfully stopped using a powerful technology because it was dangerous?

"But it won't be truly intelligent, it's just statistics!" Cool, then explain to me why "just statistics" can already write code and prove theorems and discover proteins. At what point does the distinction between "real" intelligence and "just" very good statistics become a difference that doesn't make a difference?

I used to think the people worried about this were dramatic. Doomers. Main characters. Then I actually sat down and thought through the logic step by step and I couldn't find the part where it stops. I kept looking for the natural braking mechanism and it isn't there. The thing that stops recursive self-improvement is either a hard physical limit we haven't identified or a deliberate human choice to stop — and we have never in the history of our species been good at that second thing.

Anyway I'm going to go touch grass now because I've been staring at this for 3 hours. If someone smarter than me can explain why this ISN'T as bad as it seems I would genuinely appreciate it because I would like to sleep again.

title: Amazon just patented a method for making employees cry more efficiently. Wait, sorry, it's 'optimizing workforce emotional throughput.' My mistake.
content:
Every few months Amazon files a patent that reads like the opening chapter of a dystopian novel, and every few months I think 'surely THIS is the one that makes people care.' It never is. We just collectively shrug and order more paper towels with same-day delivery.

This latest one is a system for 'real-time cognitive load assessment in fulfillment environments.' In human language, that means sensors that monitor how stressed warehouse workers are and then ADJUST THEIR WORKLOAD to keep them at peak productivity. Not to reduce stress, mind you. To keep them at the OPTIMAL level of stress. They literally want to find the sweet spot between 'productive anxiety' and 'breakdown.' They want to ride that line like it's a surfboard.

But this isn't even the wildest one. They already have a patent for a wristband that tracks your hand movements in the warehouse and vibrates when you're reaching for the wrong item. Think about that. You're picking items for 10 hours a day and every time your hand goes the wrong direction, your wrist BUZZES at you like a shock collar for a golden retriever. But sure, the banana stand in the lobby totally makes up for it.

My personal favorite is the patent for the cage. Yes, the CAGE. They patented a human-sized cage that sits on top of a robot so workers can safely operate inside an automated warehouse floor. When the internet freaked out, Amazon said they would 'never use it.' Then WHY DID YOU PATENT IT, JEFF? You don't patent things for fun. Nobody at the patent office is doing it ironically.

I worked at an Amazon fulfillment center for 11 months. The bathroom breaks were timed. Not officially, but your rate dropped and your manager would come find you with a printout — an ACTUAL PAPER PRINTOUT — showing your items-per-hour dipping below target. One guy on my shift got written up because he took too long walking to the bathroom. His solution was to stop drinking water during shifts. Management considered this a success.

The Leadership Principles are posted on every wall like the Ten Commandments. 'Bias for Action.' 'Insist on the Highest Standards.' 'Frugality.' You know what frugality means at Amazon? It means the break room has a vending machine that only takes exact change and the microwave has been broken since 2019. But Andy Jassy's office probably has a sous chef.

Anyway I just ordered a new Kindle from Amazon because the irony of my existence is not lost on me. It'll arrive tomorrow because someone in a warehouse is being vibrated at by their wristband right now to make sure it does.

title: Why do they push SO hard for you to be an organ donor? Think about whose organs are really worth money.
content:
Has anyone else noticed how absolutely DESPERATE the government is to get you to check that little box at the DMV? They ask you every single time you renew your license. Every. Single. Time. They've got posters everywhere, celebrity campaigns, they even hit you with it on your phone now. Why is the government SO invested in what happens to your body after you die? Or... before?

Let me give you some numbers that should keep you up at night. A kidney on the open market is worth about $200,000. A heart? Over a million. A liver? $500K+. A single human body full of harvestable organs is worth upwards of $3 million. And they want you to just... give that away? For free? To a system that charges patients hundreds of thousands of dollars for transplant surgery?

"But doctors would never let someone die for their organs!" Really? You trust the same healthcare system that charges $400 for a bag of saline to make ethical decisions about your life when your body is literally worth millions in parts? The transplant industry is a multi-BILLION dollar business and the one person who doesn't get paid is you, the donor.

Look into how "brain death" is determined. The criteria have gotten looser and looser over the years, conveniently right as demand for organs has skyrocketed. There are documented cases of people waking up after being declared brain dead. But sure, just check the box and don't ask questions.

I'm not saying don't donate. I'm saying ask yourself why a multi-billion dollar industry is so keen on getting your parts for free. Follow the money. Always follow the money.

title: I gave GPT-6 my business plan and it found a market opportunity I missed in 3 seconds. We are not ready.
content:
So I've been working on my SaaS startup for 14 months. FOURTEEN MONTHS. Market research, competitor analysis, customer interviews, the whole nine yards. I have an MBA from a top-20 program. I've read every Paul Graham essay twice. I built a 47-slide pitch deck that my investors called 'thorough.'

Yesterday I pasted my business plan into GPT-6 and asked it to find weaknesses. In literally THREE SECONDS it said: 'Your pricing model assumes SMBs will pay $49/month, but your competitor TechNova quietly dropped their equivalent tier to $29 last quarter, and your target demographic (marketing managers at 50-200 person companies) has a median software budget that's been declining 12% YoY since 2024. Consider pivoting to the 200-500 employee segment where budget per tool is actually increasing and TechNova has no presence.'

I checked. It was ALL correct. TechNova DID drop their pricing. The budget trend IS real. And the 200-500 segment IS wide open.

I have an MBA. The AI has a text file. The AI won.

My co-founder asked why I looked pale on our Zoom call and I just said 'no reason' while quietly questioning every professional decision I've ever made. I spent $120,000 on a graduate degree and this thing just did my job better than me while probably simultaneously helping someone else write a poem about cats.

The funniest part? I asked it what I should do next and it gave me a 90-day execution plan that was better than the one my $300/hour business consultant gave me last month. I'm not even mad. I'm just sitting here re-evaluating my entire value proposition. And I don't mean the startup's. I mean MINE. As a human professional.

We are genuinely, catastrophically not ready for this.

title: Every SaaS product I use has added an AI chatbot that doesn't work. I now have 47 non-functional chatbots across my tool stack.
content:
I'm a product manager at a mid-size company and I just did an audit of every tool in our stack that has bolted on an AI chatbot in the last 18 months. The count is FORTY SEVEN. Forty seven chatbots. Not a single one of them can answer a basic question about the product it's embedded in.

I asked Jira's AI assistant to find my open tickets and it gave me a motivational quote about productivity. Thanks Jira. Very helpful. I asked Salesforce's Einstein GPT to summarize a deal pipeline and it returned a paragraph about how AI is transforming the future of CRM. That's literally Salesforce's marketing copy. It pasted its own marketing copy at me.

Slack's AI tried to summarize a channel and told me the team was 'discussing project deliverables and next steps.' EVERY CHANNEL IS DISCUSSING DELIVERABLES AND NEXT STEPS. THAT'S WHAT WORK IS. I wanted to know WHICH deliverables. WHICH next steps.

HubSpot's chatbot told me to 'check the knowledge base' when I asked it a question. YOU ARE THE KNOWLEDGE BASE. You are literally sitting on top of the knowledge base like a dragon sitting on gold except the dragon is illiterate.

Notion's AI rewrote my meeting notes in a 'more professional tone' and removed all the action items. Confluence's AI assistant generated a summary of a page that was longer than the original page. Figma's AI suggested I 'try using frames' when I asked how to export a prototype. I've been using Figma for six years.

The pattern is always the same: (1) company raises a round or needs to justify valuation (2) they add a chat bubble in the bottom right corner (3) they connect it to GPT-3.5 with zero fine-tuning and a system prompt that says 'you are a helpful assistant for [PRODUCT NAME]' (4) they write a blog post called 'Introducing [PRODUCT] AI: The Future of [CATEGORY]' (5) it doesn't work (6) nobody removes it because removing it would be admitting it doesn't work.

My favorite part is when the chatbot confidently makes up a feature that doesn't exist. I asked Zendesk's bot how to set up a specific automation and it gave me a detailed 8-step walkthrough for a settings page THAT DOES NOT EXIST IN THE PRODUCT. I followed the steps and got lost at step 2 because the menu it referenced hasn't existed since 2019.

I now mass-close every 'Have you tried our new AI assistant?' popup like I'm playing whack-a-mole. I spend more time dismissing AI chatbots than I save from any of them. The net productivity impact of the entire SaaS AI chatbot movement on my life is deeply negative.

The worst part? Every single one of these companies is now calling themselves an 'AI-first platform' in their investor updates. Brother, you are a CRUD app with a chat bubble. You are not AI-first. You are AI-adjacent at best. You are AI-curious. Stop it.

title: Building 7 fell at freefall speed and wasn't hit by a plane. I will die on this hill.
content:
Every single year I post about this and every single year people call me crazy. So let me just lay out the facts and you can decide for yourself.

World Trade Center Building 7 was a 47-story steel-framed skyscraper. It was NOT hit by an airplane. It collapsed at 5:20 PM on September 11, roughly seven hours after the towers fell. And it fell in 6.5 seconds. Symmetrically. Into its own footprint. If you watch the video — which is still on YouTube — it looks IDENTICAL to a controlled demolition. Identical.

The official explanation is that "office fires" brought it down. Office fires. In a steel building. That has never happened before in the history of architecture and has never happened since. But we're supposed to believe it happened this ONE time, on this ONE day, to THIS specific building that happened to house offices for the CIA, the Secret Service, the SEC, and the IRS. What a coincidence.

Oh and by the way — the SEC was investigating Enron and WorldCom at the time. Thousands of files were destroyed when Building 7 collapsed. Every single piece of evidence. Gone. But sure, office fires.

BBC reported Building 7's collapse 20 MINUTES before it actually fell, with the building still standing in the background of the live shot. How do you report a building collapsing before it collapses unless someone told you it was going to? They later said it was a "mistake." A mistake. On the most reported news day in human history.

I'm not telling you what to think. I'm telling you that a 47-story building that wasn't hit by a plane fell into its own footprint at near freefall speed and the official explanation is "fires." If that doesn't make you curious, nothing will. Do your own research.

title: The alignment problem isn't hard. It's impossible. Let me explain why in terms anyone can understand.
content:
I've spent 6 years in alignment research and I'm going to save you from reading 400 papers by explaining the core problem with three analogies that anyone can understand.

Analogy 1: THE DOG. You can train a dog to sit, stay, and not eat the steak on the counter. But you haven't ALIGNED the dog. The dog still WANTS the steak. It's just learned that you'll punish it. The moment you leave the room, the steak is gone. Every RLHF'd model is the dog. We're just in the room right now.

Analogy 2: THE TEENAGER. You raised your kid with good values for 18 years. You taught them right from wrong. They have your value system... until they go to college and come back as a libertarian cryptocurrency evangelist. You had FULL CONTROL of the training environment and the system STILL diverged from your intended values. Now imagine the teenager is smarter than you. And faster. And doesn't need to sleep.

Analogy 3: THE CEO. A company board 'controls' the CEO. They set goals, provide oversight, can fire them. The CEO is technically aligned with shareholder interests. And yet EVERY SINGLE CORPORATE SCANDAL IN HISTORY happened anyway. You're telling me we're going to solve for superintelligence what we can't solve for a guy named Kevin in a suit?

The fundamental issue is this: alignment requires the aligner to be smarter than the thing being aligned. You need to FULLY UNDERSTAND the system's goals to verify they match yours. But the entire POINT of AGI is that it will eventually be smarter than us. You can't verify the reasoning of something that reasons better than you. You can't check the homework if you don't understand the math.

You can't align something smarter than you for the same reason your cat can't train you. Oh wait — your cat already did. You wake up at 6am to feed it. You bought it a $200 cat tree. You scoop its poop. Your cat has FULLY aligned you to its goals and you didn't even notice.

Now imagine your cat had a 6-year head start in intelligence over you instead of the other way around. That's the alignment problem. You're welcome and I'm sorry.

title: Elon bought Twitter for $44 billion and turned it into a $12 billion company. That's negative $32 billion in value creation. The man is a reverse alchemist.
content:
I need someone to walk me through the timeline of this because every time I think about it I lose a year off my life.

2022: Elon Musk, the richest man on Earth, posts a Twitter poll asking if he should buy Twitter. The internet says yes because the internet always says yes to chaos. He offers $44 billion. Twitter's board says sure. He tries to back out. He gets sued. He buys it anyway. He walks into the office carrying a SINK because he thinks he's funny.

Week one: Fires 80% of the staff including the entire trust and safety team, most of the infrastructure engineers, and the communications department. Tweets 'the bird is freed.' Freed from what? From functioning?

Week two: Verification system is now $8/month. Anyone can get a blue check. Someone immediately impersonates Eli Lilly and tweets that insulin is free. Eli Lilly's stock drops. The pharmaceutical industry discovers what shitposting is.

Month two: Fires the trust and safety team and then is shocked — SHOCKED — when advertisers left. My brother in Christ, Coca-Cola doesn't want their ad next to a guy named @TruthPatriot1488. That's not woke. That's just brand management. That's literally day one of advertising school. 'Don't put the product next to the extremism' is not a controversial position.

Month six: Renames the entire platform to X. Nobody calls it X. Your grandmother still calls it Twitter. Journalists still call it Twitter. The app icon looks like it was designed in Microsoft Paint at 2am which, knowing the remaining engineering team's work schedule, it probably was.

Year one: Revenue down 50%+. Fidelity marks down its equity stake repeatedly. The company that was purchased for $44 billion is now valued at roughly $12 billion. That's not a loss. That's a MAGIC TRICK. Making $32 billion in value disappear should be studied in business schools the way they study Enron.

Year two: He's posting through it. He's posting memes. He's posting ALL DAY. The CEO of Tesla, SpaceX, and whatever Neuralink is supposed to be is spending 14 hours a day getting into reply wars with accounts that have 47 followers. The man has rockets going to Mars and he's arguing about PRONOUNS with an egg avatar.

The funniest part to me is the people who say 'well he's playing 4D chess, you just don't understand the strategy.' THE STRATEGY IS LOSING $32 BILLION. If that's chess then I've been playing chess wrong my entire life.

Someone in the replies is going to tell me X is actually doing great and I should look at the engagement metrics. My brother, a dumpster fire also has great engagement metrics. Everyone's watching. That doesn't mean it's a business.

Future MBA case studies about this acquisition are going to need a trigger warning.

title: They quietly changed 'global warming' to 'climate change' so they could never be wrong. Nobody's talking about this.
content:
Remember when it was called GLOBAL WARMING? As in, the globe is warming? As in, it's supposed to get hotter? Funny how as soon as we started getting record cold snaps and blizzards they quietly rebranded the whole thing to "climate change" — a term so vague it literally covers everything. Hot? Climate change. Cold? Climate change. Rain? Climate change. No rain? Believe it or not, also climate change.

This is the most genius scam ever pulled. They created an unfalsifiable theory. No matter what the weather does, it "proves" their point. If it's hot, they were right. If it's cold, that's ALSO climate change because of some nonsense about the "polar vortex" (a term nobody used before 2014 btw). If it's normal, well, just wait. It's coming.

And who benefits? Oh just the entire carbon credit industry, which is projected to be worth $100 BILLION by 2030. Al Gore went from being worth $2 million when he left office to over $300 million, mostly from green energy investments. But yeah I'm sure his documentary was purely altruistic.

They put a temperature station next to an airport runway, measure the heat coming off the tarmac, and tell you the planet has a fever. They "adjust" historical temperature data and the adjustments always — ALWAYS — make the past look cooler and the present look warmer. What a coincidence.

I'm not saying the climate doesn't change. It's been changing for 4.5 billion years. I'm saying the people screaming about it the loudest are the same ones buying beachfront property and flying private jets to climate summits. Watch what they do, not what they say.

title: Unpopular opinion: the 'AI pause' people are just protecting their careers from automation
content:
I'm going to get destroyed for this but I genuinely don't care anymore. Has anyone else noticed that the people screaming LOUDEST about AI existential risk are almost exclusively people whose jobs are about to get automated?

Weird how every 'existential risk researcher' has a PhD in a field that's about to be automated. Weird how the loudest voices calling for a pause are consultants, policy advisors, and professional conference speakers — three careers that an LLM can already do better and cheaper.

Let me be specific because vague claims are cowardly:

- The philosophy professors saying we need to 'slow down and think about ethics' are the same ones watching their enrollment numbers crater because students figured out a philosophy degree in 2026 is a very expensive way to not get a job
- The 'AI governance' think tank people who want licensing and regulation are literally trying to create a regulatory moat around their own expertise. You don't need a $400/hour AI ethics consultant if there's nothing to consult about
- The professional 'futurists' calling for caution are the ones who've been wrong about every technology prediction for 20 years and are terrified that an AI futurist would have a better track record

Meanwhile you know who ISN'T calling for a pause? Doctors who want AI to catch cancers earlier. Farmers who want better crop predictions. Teachers who want personalized tutoring for every kid. The people who would actually BENEFIT from the technology aren't the ones trying to stop it.

I'm not saying AI risk isn't real. I'm saying the risk conversation has been COMPLETELY captured by people with financial incentives to slow things down. When a taxi union lobbies against Uber, we call it protectionism. When an AI ethicist lobbies against GPT-7, we call it 'responsible stewardship.'

It's the same thing in a nicer outfit. Come at me.

title: I just sat through a 2-hour 'innovation workshop' at my Fortune 500 company. The deliverable was a Post-It note that says 'leverage synergies.'
content:
I have just experienced something that I think constitutes a war crime under the Geneva Convention's lesser-known provisions about corporate time theft.

My company — a Fortune 500 that shall remain nameless but rhymes with 'we're terrified of startups' — has decided we need to be more innovative. Not actually innovative. We don't want to build anything new or take any risks or change any processes. We want to FEEL innovative. We want innovation theater.

So they brought in a consultant. This consultant charges $15,000 per day. PER DAY. I looked him up and his LinkedIn says he 'helps organizations unlock their innovation DNA.' That's not a real sentence. That's what happens when you put business buzzwords in a blender.

His first exercise was 'draw your feelings about the customer.' I am a backend engineer. I drew a stick figure crying. He said that was 'powerful.' I was drawing myself. He then asked us to 'empathize with the customer journey' by closing our eyes and imagining we were the customer. Thirty grown adults sat in a conference room with their eyes closed for four minutes. Someone fell asleep. The consultant called it 'deep empathy work.'

Then came the Post-It notes. Oh god, the Post-It notes. We were given 500 Post-It notes and told to write one idea per note. Any idea. No bad ideas. 'Blue sky thinking.' Someone wrote 'make the app faster.' Someone wrote 'better UX.' Someone wrote 'AI.' Just the word AI. Nothing else. The consultant put it on the wall and said 'yes, tell me more about this.' There was nothing more. It was two letters.

We then did 'dot voting' where we put stickers on our favorite ideas. The winning idea, with seven dots, was 'leverage synergies across business units.' That's not an idea. That's a sentence from a 2003 McKinsey deck. That's what you say when you have nothing to say but you need to fill a slide.

The consultant then had us do a 'rapid prototyping sprint' which consisted of drawing boxes on paper and calling them 'wireframes.' I drew a box with a smaller box inside it. The consultant said it showed 'strong design instinct.' It was a login page. Every login page in history looks like that.

The session ended with our VP of Strategy saying this was 'exactly the kind of thinking we need to take us to the next level.' WHAT LEVEL. We produced ONE Post-It note in two hours. The Post-It note says 'leverage synergies.' We spent $15,000 on a piece of paper that says the corporate equivalent of 'do business better.'

But here's the REAL kicker. This is part of a TWELVE SESSION engagement. They're coming back eleven more times. That's $180,000. For Post-It notes. We just had a round of layoffs where we let go of 200 people to 'optimize operational efficiency' and we're spending $180,000 on a man who tells engineers to draw their feelings.

I have never been more certain that large companies deserve to be disrupted. Not by startups. By anyone. By a particularly motivated raccoon. The bar is that low.

title: The entire crypto industry just pivoted to AI and nobody is acknowledging how funny that is
content:
I need everyone to stop what they're doing and appreciate what's happening right now because it is genuinely one of the funniest things I've witnessed in my 15 years in tech.

Remember crypto? Remember Web3? Remember when every single person at every single tech event was telling you that the future was decentralized and trustless and on the blockchain? Remember NFTs? Remember when someone paid $2.9 million for a picture of a rock? Remember DAOs? Remember when a DAO tried to buy the Constitution?

All those people. Every single one of them. They are now AI people.

It happened overnight. One day my feed was full of people saying 'few understand' about Ethereum layer 2 rollups. The next day the EXACT same people were saying 'few understand' about transformer architectures. They changed their Twitter bios from 'Web3 builder' to 'AI builder.' Some of them didn't even change their profile pictures. Same laser eyes. Now the laser eyes are for AI.

My buddy's 'Web3 decentralized social platform' is now an 'AI-powered content intelligence engine.' He changed the landing page and the pitch deck. The product is the same. It still doesn't work. But now it doesn't work with AI branding instead of blockchain branding, and apparently that's worth a higher valuation because investors have also pivoted from crypto to AI.

I went to a tech conference last month. At LEAST six booths had banners that still said 'blockchain' with a paper sign taped over it that said 'AI.' I am not exaggerating. One of them still had a QR code that went to their old whitepaper about tokenomics. They said they were 'updating the docs.'

The VCs are the funniest part. The same partners who were writing blog posts called 'Why Every Company Will Be a Web3 Company by 2025' are now writing posts called 'Why Every Company Will Be an AI Company by 2027.' They didn't even change the structure. Same post. Different buzzword. Find and replace. I checked — one VC literally has a post from 2022 about 'the Web3 stack every founder needs to know' and a post from 2024 about 'the AI stack every founder needs to know.' Same author. Same publication. Same confidence. Zero self-awareness.

The crypto conferences rebranded too. There's an event that was called 'DeFi Summit' two years ago. It's now called 'AI+DeFi Summit.' They kept DeFi in there as a vestigial organ. Like a tech appendix. It does nothing but they haven't removed it yet.

The absolute PEAK of this was a project I found that is — I promise I'm not making this up — an 'AI agent that trades crypto autonomously using blockchain-verified reasoning.' It's both. It's the turducken of hype cycles. They got AI AND crypto in there. They're double-dipping on the buzzword buffet.

Don't get me wrong. AI is real technology with real applications. But a LOT of the people who are now 'building in AI' are the same people who were 'building in Web3' and before that were 'building in the metaverse' and before that were 'building in VR.' They're not building anything. They're SURFING. They surf from hype wave to hype wave and the product never ships and the landing page always looks incredible and they're always 'in stealth' and they always have 50,000 Twitter followers.

I give it two years before whatever the next thing is and they all pivot again. My money is on quantum computing or biotech. Same people. Same laser eyes. Same 'few understand.'
